title: Project a function in ten lines
summary: Build a mesh, project a smooth function onto the lowest-order space and read the value at a point.
assumes: A smooth function of a point; a tetrahedral mesh.
cost: Milliseconds for a mesh of a few hundred cells.

title: Use your own mesh, and see what bad input does
summary: Pass vertex and tetrahedron arrays from Gmsh, TetGen or your own code, check them, and find the cell that contains a point.
assumes: Positively oriented tetrahedra that meet in whole faces.
cost: Linear in the number of cells.

title: Read a mesh from Gmsh
summary: Load a .msh file (ASCII, format 2.2 or 4.1, first-order tetrahedra) with parseGmsh and use it like any other mesh. What cannot be used is an error that says why.
assumes: An ASCII .msh file with first-order tetrahedra; no binary, no hexahedra, prisms, pyramids or second-order elements.
cost: Linear in the size of the file.

title: The four form degrees
summary: A potential, an edge field, a flux and a density: what each one projects to and where it lives.
assumes: Input regular enough for point values, edge integrals and face fluxes (the canonical operator).
cost: Microseconds per point once the projector is built.

title: A field that is infinite at a vertex
summary: The canonical interpolation refuses it; the stable operator integrates against a weight and stays finite. This is what the bounded operators are for.
assumes: A field in L2, finite on the boundary (the stable operator).
cost: Milliseconds per entity: a local solve around each one, cached.

title: Check that the projection commutes with the derivative
summary: The gradient of the projection is the projection of the gradient, so curl-free fields stay curl-free. Two ways to see it.
assumes: Canonical operator: smooth input. Bounded operator: any input in L2. The trace-preserving and stable operators commute for fields whose boundary trace is a lowest-order trace; outside that class commuting fails (by about 5e-3 on a 4x4x4 cube), which the papers' proof does not cover (see Limits).
cost: The bounded operator solves a local problem per entity.

title: Keep the values on the boundary
summary: Which operators reproduce boundary values exactly, and which trade that for needing less of the input.
assumes: Stable operator: finite point values on the boundary. Trace-preserving operator: only L2 data near it. The trace-preserving operator above the lowest order is validated at degrees 1 and 2 on cubes; its stability constant there is measured only in part (see Validation).
cost: The trace-preserving operator costs more per boundary entity.

title: Refine where it matters
summary: Bisect the cells around a feature, keep the mesh conforming, and watch the error near the feature fall.
assumes: A conforming mesh; marked cells chosen by you.
cost: Each refinement rebuilds the topology: linear in the cells.

title: Time-dependent data
summary: Locate the evaluation points once, then project each new time step cheaply.
assumes: Fixed evaluation points inside the mesh.
cost: Point location once; then a few microseconds per point and step.

title: Use all the cores
summary: Project one field at many points on worker threads, or compute the coefficients of a bounded operator on a pool. The result is bitwise the same as on one thread.
assumes: Node.js; the field is a module with a default export.
cost: Speed-up is modest and machine dependent (3.4 times on 8 workers on the measured machine): each worker computes its own weights.

title: Higher polynomial degree
summary: Canonical interpolation of any degree, the locally bounded higher-order projection, and the trace-preserving operator above the lowest order.
assumes: A mesh fine enough that the extended stars are balls (at least about 6 cells per side for a cube).
cost: Seconds per weight at degree 1; the trace-preserving operator costs seconds to tens of seconds per point near the boundary. Its stability above the lowest order is measured only in part (see Validation).
